source_refs.note: Exercise 4.1, Question 5: radioactive decay (Hint); book p. 128, answers p. 303 (PDF 305)

blocks.prompt: 5 Let \(N\) denote the amount of radioactive substance present at time \(t\). Construct a differential equation that models the radioactive decay of the substance. Hint: (Radioactive decay is a natural process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by emitting radiation. The rate at which a radioactive substance decays is proportional to the amount of the substance present at any given time.)
blocks.explanation:
A modelling question: the hint says the decay rate is proportional to the amount \(N\).
Decay means \(N\) decreases, so the rate \(\frac{dN}{dt}\) is negative.
steps:
Given: amount \(N(t)\); rate of decay proportional to \(N\).
To find: a differential equation for \(N\).
Method: the decay model \(\frac{dN}{dt} = -kN\) with \(k > 0\).

Write the proportionality
\[\dfrac{dN}{dt} \propto N\]
Why: more atoms means more of them break up each second.

Fix the sign
\(N\) decreases, so \(\frac{dN}{dt} < 0\). With a positive constant \(k\) (the decay constant):
\[\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -kN\]
\[\dfrac{dN}{dt} + kN = 0,\quad k > 0\]
Why: this is Example 1's model \(\frac{dP}{dt} = kP\) with a negative constant, which the book's Observation calls decay.

Check:
\(N = N_{0}e^{-kt}\) gives \(\frac{dN}{dt} = -kN_{0}e^{-kt} = -kN\) (sympy); \(N\) decreases towards 0 but never becomes negative.
blocks.final_answer: \(\dfrac{dN}{dt} = -kN\), i.e. \(\dfrac{dN}{dt} + kN = 0\), where \(k > 0\) is the decay constant.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(\frac{dN}{dt} = -kT,\ k > 0\). There is no \(T\) in this question: the decay rate depends on the amount \(N\). The correct equation is \(\frac{dN}{dt} = -kN,\ k > 0\).
